Yet, the Dharma is fundamentally ineffable; fearing that one might grasp at or become attached to it, it is said to be "not the foremost pāramitā.
However, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken of, and thus it is said, "this is named the foremost pāramitā."

8. Severing and Maintaining the Explanation of Doubts Regarding Not Yet Being Liberated from the Fruits of Suffering. This doubt arises from the preceding passage on the sacrifice of one’s body: “Subhūti!...”
The perfection of patience, the Tathāgata says, is not the perfection of patience.
Why is this? Subhūti!
When I was formerly cut and mangled in body by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.

Why is this? When my limbs and joints were severed in the past, if there had been in me any perception of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

Subhūti! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience; throughout all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
"Patience (kṣānti) is one of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). To accept [suffering] with composure is called patience; to be harmed or injured is called insult.

As stated previously, the meritorious retribution of sacrificing one's body and life is a cause for the suffering of birth and death, and does not equal the merit of upholding and expounding [this teaching]."
Why is it that this patience in practice also involves relinquishing body and life without becoming a cause for suffering?
It is because one is able to realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and reach the further shore.
To say that this is not the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is to eliminate attachment.
Because the Buddha practiced such patience in the past, he cites the incident involving King Kali as proof.
In Sanskrit, *kali* means "extremely wicked" in Chinese. In a previous life, the Buddha was once a rishi practicing the Way in the mountains.

When a king went hunting and saw him, he was displeased and consequently cut off his ears and nose and severed his hands and feet. At that time, the rishi felt not the slightest resentment; through the power of loving-kindness and forbearance, his body was restored to its former state. This was because he had thoroughly realized that the four marks—the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—are all empty. Thus, far from suffering, he even experienced bliss.
Furthermore, the citation of his past five hundred lifetimes as the Sage of Forbearance (Kṣāntivādin) serves to demonstrate that the practice of patience does not pertain to a single lifetime alone.
"Therefore, Subhūti! [he said].

A bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor should they give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling; therefore, the Buddha said that the Bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell upon form when practicing giving.

Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner. The Tathāgata says that all marks are non-marks, and he also says that all sentient beings are non-sentient beings.

The Buddha practiced patience throughout successive lifetimes and, by virtue of non-self, attained Bodhi; therefore, one who has resolved upon the mind of Bodhi must distance themselves from all marks. To be free from marks is precisely to not dwell within the six sense objects, such as form and the rest.
One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere; when the mind dwells nowhere, one is able to abide in Bodhi. If the mind has a dwelling place, then one does not abide in the Buddha-way.

All the practices of the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) performed by a Bodhisattva should be free from signs (*nimitta*). Since form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of the six sense objects and giving (*dāna*) is the first of the six perfections, it is said that "one should not dwell on form while practicing giving. Such practice of giving is for the benefit of all sentient beings; if one harbors a mind of giver and receiver, it is not "dwelling nowhere."
Because he was again commanded to put it on, it is said that it is "neither a mark nor a sentient being.
9. Dispelling the Doubt That the Realizer Lacks Substance and Is Not the Cause. This doubt arises from the preceding discussion on practicing giving for the benefit of living beings: "Subhūti!..."
The Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception, and speaks without contradiction. Subhūti,
as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.

The Tathāgata has realized the sublime fruit of awakening in accordance with reality, which is beyond verbal expression; for what reason, then, do you repeatedly extol the merit of upholding and explaining this [sūtra] as superior to the blessings of other forms of giving?

However, the Buddha realizes that which is not realized and speaks that which is not spoken; yet what he realizes and what he speaks never fail to accord with principle. Fearing that Subhūti had not yet grasped this meaning, the Buddha spoke again, saying: "This is the truth," and so forth.
One who speaks the truth speaks of the Buddha’s bodhi;
one who speaks reality speaks of the Dharma of the Hīnayāna;
one who speaks as it is speaks of the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
"Non-discrepant speech" refers to speaking in accordance with what has been received;
"non-deceptive speech" refers to not deceiving sentient beings.
The commentary by Jieyi does not contain this sentence.
Regarding "neither real nor unreal": the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is fundamentally beyond verbal expression, and is thus said to be "not real";
yet, because he teaches in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, it is said to be "not unreal."
10. Resolving Doubts Regarding Whether True Suchness Is Attained or Not Attained. This doubt arises from the preceding section on not abiding in signs: “Subhūti! ...”
If a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing;
if a bodhisattva does not dwell upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person with eyes, when the light of the sun shines, seeing all manner of forms.

"The Sages are named for the unconditioned True Suchness (*tathatā*); yet, since the essence of True Suchness pervades all times and all places, why is it that some sentient beings attain it while others do not?"
It is simply that the mind has the distinction between abiding in phenomena (*dharma*) and not abiding in phenomena. "Abiding" means attachment.

For example, if one practices giving without realizing the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), it is called "abiding in phenomena. When the mind abides in phenomena, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is not accomplished; it is like entering darkness where nothing can be seen.

If one realizes that the three spheres are empty in essence, the mind has no place to abide; this constitutes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), just as a person with eyes perceives various forms and appearances within the sunlight.

“Subhūti! In a future age, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall all achieve immeasurable and boundless merit.”

It is said that if there are those in future ages who receive, uphold, read, and recite this, the Buddha’s eye and the Buddha’s wisdom will fully know and see them; since they practice such superior causes, they will surely achieve wondrous fruits, and thus it is said that they shall accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.

“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the middle part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the latter part of the day, likewise gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—continuing in this manner, giving away their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas—if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, did not oppose it with faith, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former; how much more so if they were to copy it, receive and uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it to others?”
The first watch of the day consists of the hours of Tiyu, Maowu, and Chen;
the middle watch of the day consists of the hours of Si, Wu, and Wei;
and the latter watch of the day consists of the hours of Shen, You, and Xu.
In this way, one might give away immeasurable bodies three times each day for immeasurable eons while practicing generosity.

Such a thing certainly does not exist in the world; yet the Buddha established this analogy to illustrate the superiority of the merit born from hearing this sutra and giving rise to faith—how much more so for those who write it down, uphold it, recite it, and explain it?
The power of faith is called receiving; the power of mindfulness is called upholding; facing the text is called reading; reciting from memory is called chanting.
What is meant by copying, receiving, upholding, reading, and chanting refers to one's own practice;
explaining it for others refers to transforming others.

“Subhūti! To speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit; it has been taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it for others, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall all achieve immeasurable, ineffable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Such persons as these shall indeed be carrying the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span; they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.

The essence of this Prajñā is fundamentally beyond words and thought; its merit is so vast that it cannot be measured or described, and it is not something those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle can hear. Therefore, it is said: "It is taught for those who set out upon the Great Vehicle; it is taught for those who set out upon the Supreme Vehicle."
Those who "set forth the Mahāyāna" refers generally to those belonging to the three teachings of the Vaipulya gate;
those who "set forth the Supreme Vehicle" specifically refers to those of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] who are capable of generating faith and understanding.
When such a person practices this Dharma, they will achieve inconceivable merit; therefore, they are able to shoulder the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle are unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain it to others, because they are attached to the four views. "Subhūti!
Wherever this sutra exists, it should be honored by all the worlds—devas, humans, and asuras."
"You should know that this place is a stūpa; you must all pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it, scattering various flowers and incense upon that spot.
A stūpa is a place where śarīras are enshrined; whether they be devas, humans, or asuras, they should certainly honor and serve it with reverence.
"Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā sūtra volume may be located, that place is a true stupa containing the relics of the Dharma-body;
how could it not be revered? Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If good sons or good daughters accept, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, yet are treated with contempt by others, their karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are extinguished by virtue of being so treated by others in the present life; they shall thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Those who uphold and recite this sutra should be treated with reverence by others; yet if they are instead treated with contempt, it is because their past karmic offenses are destined to bring about an evil retribution. It is solely due to the power of the sutra that they merely suffer such contempt; and because they are so treated, their sins are extinguished, and they shall attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, the merit of upholding this sutra may indeed be called great.

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, during immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, none of whom I failed to honor.”

Furthermore, if there should be anyone in the final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain shall surpass the merit from my own offerings to all Buddhas; even a hundredth part, a thousand-million-billionth part, or even any calculation or analogy cannot reach it.
*Asaṃkhyeya* is translated as "innumerable time.
Regarding *nayuta*: ten billion is a *lakṣa*; ten *lakṣas* is a *koṭi*; and ten *koṭis* is a *nayuta*.

The Tathāgata made offerings to countless Buddhas prior to the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara; his merit may indeed be called profound and vast. Yet he stated that it does not equal the merit of those who uphold this sutra in the final age, for upholding this sutra can give rise to understanding and realization, leading to the attainment of Bodhi.

Although making offerings to the Buddha does induce meritorious retribution, it pertains merely to the realm of phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, the merit of upholding this sutra exceeds it by a factor of hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, such that the former does not equal even one part in a hundred thousand million.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy," this is because the merit of phenomenal characteristics is a dharma that can be conceptualized, whereas the wondrous wisdom of Prajñā transcends subject and object and severs all dualistic oppositions, rendering it impossible to conceive or calculate.

“Subhūti! If I were to fully describe the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age at the end of time, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and, filled with doubt, would not believe it.”
"Subhūti! You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
This sutra cannot be upheld or recited by those who lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna; how then could ordinary people hear of the merit induced by such upholding and recitation?

Hearing this, one would surely harbor doubts and fail to believe; therefore, I have not explained it in full detail, for the meaning and purport of this sutra, as well as its karmic retribution, are inconceivable.

11. Severing the Doubt Concerning Abiding in and Subduing the Notion of Self. This doubt arises from the preceding passages concerning the absence of marks such as self and person. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”
"Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi: how should they abide?
How should they subdue their minds?"
Why is it that Subhūti, having first heard this meaning, asks again at this point?
Although the phrasing of the question is the same, its intent is different; for what he asks concerns nothing other than abiding in the Mahāyāna and subduing the deluded mind.
The intent of the first question was merely to inquire about the dharma that can abide and the dharma that can subdue;

the intent of this [second] question is that if one thinks, "I can abide" or "I can subdue," such conceptual discrimination will obstruct the realization of the true path of non-abiding; therefore, this question is raised once again.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should give rise to this thought:
'I should bring all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*)."
"Having brought all sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to final nirvana.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
If a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti!
"In reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The meaning of this passage is the same as the preceding one; however, while the previous section refuted emotional attachments to reveal wisdom—where the attachments refuted were the coarse grasping at the four marks such as self and person, and the wisdom revealed was the true wisdom of *prajñā*—from this point onward, wisdom is forgotten to reveal the principle, thereby refuting the subtle grasping at the four marks such as self and person. Through this, one gradually enters the stages of sainthood from the level of worthiness (*śaikṣa*).

12. Severing the Cause of Buddhahood: The Doubt Regarding the Existence of Bodhisattvas. This doubt arises from the preceding [point] that there is truly no one who gives rise to the bodhicitta. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara that constituted *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Since it was previously stated that "in reality, there is no dharma by which one generates the mind of enlightenment," this implies that if there is no one who generates the mind, there is no Bodhisattva. If there is no Bodhisattva, how could Śākyamuni have been named Sudhana at the place of Dīpaṃkara, having spread his hair to cover the mud, practiced the conduct of a Bodhisattva, and received the prediction of enlightenment?
The Buddha, fearing that Subhūti might harbor such a doubt in secret, raised it as a question:
"No, World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
Subhūti’s intended answer was this:
At that time, Subhūti attained nothing at all; free from all conceptual discrimination, he received the prediction because he realized the non-existence of phenomena.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment.
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for this reason Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni."
"Subhūti, having realized that dharmas are unattainable, the Buddha approved his statement, saying: 'So it is, so it is.

That he further repeated this instruction was because he wished to ensure that Subhūti understood that dharmas are unattainable and would profoundly accord with the ultimate truth; thus, he received the prediction of enlightenment."

Indeed, the wondrous fruit realized by the Tathāgata is a dharma-gate inherently possessed within the mind-ground; it is free from all names and characteristics, and while there is no giving or receiving within it, it is spoken of in terms of giving and receiving.

13. Severing Doubt Regarding the Non-existence of Causes Eliminates Doubt Regarding the Buddha-Dharma. Thirteen: Severing Doubt Regarding the Non-existence of Causes Eliminates Doubt Regarding the Buddha-Dharma. This doubt arises from the previous [section] concerning Śākyamuni’s practice of causes under Dīpaṃkara, which was said to be "truly without attainment. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena.
If someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," [they speak falsely].
"Subhūti! In reality, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'.
As for the phrase "Why is this?", it is an interrogative expression used to raise a question.
As stated previously:
"In reality, there is no dharma that attains the fruit of bodhi; therefore, I received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara.
Consequently, a doubt arises: if there is no fruit of Buddhahood, how could there be Buddha-dharmas?
The commentary states:
"Tathāgata means the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Suchness refers to true suchness (bhūtatathatā); it is called "true" because it is not false, and "such" because it is not different.

This essence of true suchness penetrates the three periods of time and extends throughout the ten directions; it is neither empty nor existent, neither changing nor shifting, and is named the nature of the Tathāgata. If there is anything to be attained, it is not the Bodhi of the Buddha.
“Subhūti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata contains neither reality nor unreality; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.”
"Subhūti! That which is called 'all dharmas' is precisely not all dharmas; therefore it is named 'all dharmas.
What is attained is the realization through the forgetting of conceptual thought."
That which is without reality is not a conditioned characteristic;
that which is without falsehood is the essence of *tathatā*.

Yet this *tathatā* does not exist as a separate phenomenon; rather, it is precisely all phenomena, such as form and so forth, when they are free from intrinsic nature and free from characteristics—this is called the essence of *tathatā*. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can realize this.
Therefore, all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Although the essence of true suchness is not separate from all dharmas, it likewise cannot be grasped or clung to; thus it is said:
"It is not all dharmas; it is called 'all dharmas' [only as a designation]."
“Subhūti! It is, for example, like a human body that is large and tall. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large, it is not a large body; it is called a ‘large body.

Previously, it was stated that the essence of True Suchness realized by the Tathāgata pervades all places and may thus be described as vast and great. Furthermore, fearing that Subhūti might give rise to a view of such vastness, the Buddha again employs a metaphor to inquire of him, saying:
"It is like a person whose body is tall and large.
Due to this analogy, Subhūti attained realization and said:
"It is not a large body; it is called a 'large body' [only by name]."
The treatise states:
"The 'Great Body' has two meanings:
first, pervading all places, which is the Dharma-body; second, having great merit, which is the Reward-body."
These two bodies are both free from all marks; therefore, they are called "non-existent. 14.

Dispelling Doubts Regarding There Being No One Who Delivers Beings or Adorns Buddha-lands. This doubt is the same as the twelfth doubt; it both originates from and follows upon the eleventh doubt concerning the fact that there is truly no dharma by which one awakens the mind [to enlightenment]. "Subhūti!..."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: if they should say,
"I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then they cannot be called a Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti,
in reality there is no dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva."
Therefore, the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva should speak thus:
"One who thinks, 'I shall adorn the Buddha-lands,' is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this? "
The Tathāgata says that the adornment of Buddha-fields is itself not adornment; it is called "adornment" only as a designation.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly a bodhisattva.
In the Dharma-realm, all is interpenetrating and the body and land are equal; since there is not even a Buddha-way to be accomplished, how could there be sentient beings to be saved?

Thus, to give rise to the mind of saving sentient beings and to practice for the purpose of adorning the land is merely the view of an ordinary person, and cannot be called the state of a Bodhisattva.
Ultimately, what kind of mind must arise to be called a bodhisattva?
Therefore, it is said that one who is able to penetrate the dharma of non-self is a true bodhisattva. 15.

Dispelling the Doubt that the Buddhas Do Not Perceive All Dharmas. This doubt arises from the preceding point that bodhisattvas do not see sentient beings to be saved or buddha-fields to be purified. [The Buddha said: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
"It is so, World-Honored One."
"The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. "Subhūti,
what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand?”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has said that this is sand. "Subhūti!"
What do you think?

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River; and suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would these not be very many?
“Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Tathāgata fully knows all the various kinds of minds belonging to all sentient beings within those lands.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are non-minds; it is for this reason they are called "mind. Why is that?
"Subhūti! The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.

As previously stated, not seeing those as sentient beings, not seeing oneself as a bodhisattva, and not seeing the purification of buddha-fields—thus, not seeing any dharmas is what is called a Buddha, a Tathāgata.
However, the Tathāgata is endowed with the five eyes; how could it be that he sees nothing at all?
The five eyes are the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
An ancient worthy’s verse says:

“The divine eye is unimpeded, while the fleshly eye is hindered and lacks penetration; the dharma-eye observes only the conventional, while the wisdom-eye clearly perceives emptiness; the Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns, illuminating diverse forms as ultimately identical.”
These five eyes pervade all ten realms, yet they differ in their degree of excellence; as stated in the sutras, those five eyes possessed by the Tathāgata are none other than the Buddha-eye.
The Tathāgata knows and perceives the minds of all sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Yet, when it is said that the various inverted minds of sentient beings are "not-mind," this refers to the fact that deluded consciousness is fundamentally empty.
That which is called "mind" is the non-extinction of True Suchness (tathatā).
Why is this so? The following section interrogates and explains the reason why it is not [ordinary] mind.

For the mind of the three periods of time—having already ceased in the past, not yet arrived in the future, and not abiding in the present—is entirely a matter of false arising and ceasing; therefore, it cannot be found when sought.
16. Severing Doubts Regarding the Inversion of the Mind in the Case of Merit. This doubt arises from the inversion of the mind during the preceding stage of mental abiding. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit?"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
By these causes and conditions, this person would gain exceedingly great merit. "Subhūti!"
"If merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains much merit;
because merit is non-substantial, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit.
Previously it was stated that for sentient beings to have a mind that dwells in attachment is an inversion; however, since merit is created by the mind, how could it also be an inversion?
If this were so, how could they be called wholesome dharmas?
Fearing that this doubt might remain latent, the Buddha resolved it:
"Regarding the reality of merit: if one practices giving while abiding in signs, it becomes a cause for outflows, and its merit is meager."
For one who lacks [the notion of] merit, giving while detached from signs becomes a cause for outflow-free (anāsrava) fruition; thus, their merit is vast.
This is because they do not dwell upon signs, their minds are free from inversion, and every merit they perform is nothing other than wholesome dharma.

17. Dispelling the Doubt as to How There Can Be Marks and Signs if [Dharmas] Are Non-existent. This doubt arises from the preceding statement that "the Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas," followed by: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can the Buddha be seen by means of his physical body?
"No, World-Honored One."
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the body of perfect form. Why is this?
The Tathāgata says that the body of perfect form is itself not a body of perfect form; it is merely designated as "the body of perfect form."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! One should not see the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this? Because..."
“The Tathāgata says that being endowed with all marks is itself not being endowed with them; it is merely called ‘being endowed with all marks.

Previously, it was stated that what the Buddhas realize is the unconditioned Dharma; how then can the Buddha’s body possess the eighty minor marks and thirty-two major marks such that they are visible?
To sever this doubt, this question was posed.

Subhūti thus realized that while the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is certainly not a physical form that can be seen, it is likewise never separate from physical form such that it could not be seen; therefore, he said: "It is not a complete physical body, yet it is called a complete physical body."

It is precisely because it is not the fulfillment of the various marks that it is called the fulfillment of the various marks; this is truly because the unconditioned essence of the Dharmakāya gives rise to the function of the marks and signs of the Nirmāṇakāya.
Therefore, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is itself the dharma-body (dharmakāya); it is formless yet possesses form, and possesses form yet is formless;
it is invisible yet visible, and visible yet invisible.
18. Dispelling the Doubt as to How One Who Is Bodiless Can Preach the Dharma. This doubt arises from the preceding point that the physical marks of the body cannot be perceived: “Subhūti!...”
Do not think that the Tathāgata has this thought:
"I shall preach some dharma.
Do not entertain such a thought.
Why is this? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, they misrepresent me, for they do not understand what I have taught. Subhūti!
“The one who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma.
Since it is said that the physical marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s form-body cannot be perceived, how can he expound the Dharma for others?

However, the Tathāgata’s compassionate vows are profound and weighty; he responds according to the conditions of those who perceive him. He speaks without speaking, and his speaking is itself non-speaking. Failing to comprehend this meaning constitutes slandering the Buddha.

"To say that there is no dharma that can be taught is what is called 'teaching the Dharma'"; this means that once one is free from the attachment to intrinsic nature, it does not hinder one from teaching in accordance with that very nature.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma taught, will give rise to faith?
Subhūti was foremost among those who understood emptiness; because he was in accord with the wisdom of the emptiness of *prajñā* and took wisdom as his life, he was called "Life of Wisdom."

It was previously stated that the body is the "body of no-body" and the Dharma is the "teaching of no-teaching"; since both the body and the teaching are so wondrous as to be difficult to believe and difficult to understand, this doubt has arisen.
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! They are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings."

"Sentient beings are of two kinds: the noble and the ordinary. Among them, ordinary sentient beings cannot give rise to faith in this Prajñā; only those with the body of a noble one are able to believe and understand it."
To say they are "not sentient beings" means they are not ordinary, mundane beings;
to say they are "not non-sentient beings" means they are not those who lack the nature of the noble body (*āryakāya*).
Those with the nature of the noble body are precisely the individuals possessing the capacity for the Mahāyāna; how could they be regarded as ordinary beings incapable of generating faith?
Fearing that Subhūti might still not have realized this, the following text further interrogates and explains it:
"For what reason, Subhūti?"
"Sentient beings, sentient beings—what the Tathāgata calls 'sentient beings' are not sentient beings; they are merely named 'sentient beings.
The phrase "sentient beings, sentient beings" reiterates the preceding statement that they are neither non-sentient beings nor not non-sentient beings.

When the Tathāgata says that "what is not a sentient being is called a sentient being," he means that it is not an ordinary, mundane sentient being, but rather a sentient being who possesses the essence of a sage and is capable of generating faith and understanding.

19. Doubt regarding how one cultivates and realizes the Dharma when there is no dharma to be attained. This doubt arises from the previous twelfth and thirteenth doubts concerning the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* when there is no dharma. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Subhūti! In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; it is for this reason that it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since it was previously stated that there is truly no dharma by which one attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, how can there nonetheless be cultivation and realization?
Thus, he asks out of doubt.
The Buddha’s response consists of three parts:

The first answer is that the non-attainment of any dharma constitutes perfect enlightenment; the second answer is that equality constitutes perfect enlightenment; the third answer is that the cultivation of wholesome dharmas through both the primary and auxiliary practices constitutes perfect enlightenment.
The first answer may be understood according to the text.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This second answer establishes equality as perfect enlightenment.
"By practicing all wholesome dharmas while being without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Subhūti! What are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as 'wholesome dharmas.
This is the third answer, concerning the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment through the cultivation of wholesome dharmas by means of both the primary and auxiliary practices.

Regarding "the primary and the auxiliary": "primary" refers to the correct contemplation of emptiness and the four marks; "auxiliary" refers to the supportive conditions for cultivating all wholesome dharmas.

The first answer, that there is no dharma to be attained as true awakening, means that realizing delusion is itself the truth. The second, that equality is true awakening, means that dharmas have neither high nor low. The third, that the primary and auxiliary together constitute true awakening, means cultivating goodness while remaining detached from marks; because one is detached from marks, it is called a "wholesome dharma."
20. Severing Doubt Regarding the Indeterminate and Non-causal as Taught. This doubt arises from the preceding cultivation of wholesome dharmas: “Subhūti!...”

If someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a heap of the seven treasures in alms, and if another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even a single four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the former merit would not equal one hundredth part of the latter; it would not equal one part in a hundred thousand million billion, nor could it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.

Since it was previously stated that bodhi is attained by practicing wholesome dharmas, one might harbor the doubt: "Are not the dharmas taught by the Buddha indeterminate (avyākṛta), such that they cannot lead to the attainment of bodhi?

To prevent this suspicion, the Buddha compares the vast quantity and magnitude of a heap of the seven treasures, as large as Mount Sumeru, given as alms throughout the great trichiliocosm, with the merit of upholding and reciting these four lines of verse; he shows that the former does not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the latter.

Regarding the Dharma that is taught: the Buddha is, in truth, free from the characteristics of verbal expression; because he is free from such characteristics, he is able to act as the cause for bodhi. Thus, the verse by Maitreya says:
"Although it is an indeterminate dharma..."
"And it is said that this is its cause. That is itself bodhi. 21.
Resolving Doubts Regarding the Equality of Severance. This doubt arises from the nineteenth doubt concerning the equality of dharmas: "Subhūti!..."
What do you think? You should not suppose that the Tathāgata thinks:
"I shall deliver sentient beings."
"Subhūti! Do not conceive such a thought. Why is that?
In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti! When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does not speak of a self; yet ordinary people think there is a self. Subhūti!
"Ordinary beings," the Tathāgata says, "are not actually ordinary beings.
Since you have stated that all phenomena are equal and without distinction of high or low, why does the Tathāgata nonetheless deliver sentient beings?
Therefore, the verse says:
"In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings; for their names are identical to those of the aggregates, and they do not depart from the Dharma-realm.

"Name" refers to the conventional designation of sentient beings, while "aggregates" refers to the substantial dharmas of the five aggregates. Since both these conventional designations and substantial dharmas are themselves the Dharma-realm, it is said that they do not depart from the Dharma-realm.
Since one has already realized the Dharma-realm, where ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, how could there be any sentient beings to be saved?
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha does not save sentient beings.
If the Tathāgata were to say:
"To say, 'I am the one who delivers' and 'sentient beings are those to be delivered,' is to be attached to the four marks.
By being free from these four marks, one delivers without delivering, and delivers while not delivering; this is what the Tathāgata means when he says there is a self—it is the true self."
Thus, that which is "not having a self" does not refer to a false self;
rather, it refers to the "self" of ordinary beings, which is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Regarding those who are not ordinary beings, the Treatise says:
“Non-arising” means not giving rise to the dharmas of the noble ones; this refers to the ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*). 22.

Dispelling the Doubt that the True Buddha Can Be Known by Comparing Physical Marks. This doubt arises from the seventeenth doubt, which states that the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the physical body or its various marks. [The Buddha said: “Subhūti!...”
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, so it is; one perceives the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would be the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by form, Or seeks me by sound,..."
"Such people walk upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The thirty-two marks refer to the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
To contemplate the Tathāgata is to contemplate the Tathāgata of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
The questioner’s intention was:
"Can one perceive the Dharma-body within the marks and signs of the Response-body?
Subhūti, knowing that the marks and signs of the Response-body flow forth from the Dharma-body, and that seeing these marks and signs is itself seeing the Dharma-body, replied:

"So it is, so it is. The Buddha, fearing again that Subhūti might become attached to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and fail to realize the essence of the Dharma, further raised the difficulty of the wheel-turning monarch being identical to the Tathāgata. Subhūti, understanding the intent behind the Buddha's challenge, replied:
"The Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks."

Thereupon, the Buddha spoke a verse to substantiate this: "The essence of the Dharma-body is certainly not separate from sound and form; yet ordinary beings fall into hearing and seeing, thereby practicing a deviant path and unable to perceive the Tathāgata."

23. Dispelling the Doubt that Attaining Buddhahood is Irrelevant to the Marks of Auspiciousness. This doubt arises from the preceding statement: "Subhūti, one should not perceive the Buddha by means of his physical marks."
Subhūti, if you should think:
"The Tathāgata does not attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection," [you would be mistaken]. Subhūti!
Do not harbor this thought:
"The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks that are fully complete. Subhūti!
If you should think: "One who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* teaches the annihilation of all phenomena," do not entertain such a thought.
Why is this? Because those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
Does this mean that the merit cultivated by a Bodhisattva does not serve as a cause for attaining *bodhi*, nor does it result in karmic retribution?
To sever this doubt, he told him: "Do not harbor such a thought.
The Tathāgata does not attain bodhi by means of the marks of perfection; these marks of perfection are themselves the marks of merit."

In essence, the causes of merit cultivated in the Mahāyāna and the fruits of merit attained therein merely involve the departure from signs of grasping; they do not share the view of annihilation found in the Hīnayāna. Therefore it is said:
"Regarding dharmas, I do not speak of a mark of annihilation."
Furthermore, he provides an analogy to explain:

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and give them as a gift, and if another person were to realize that all phenomena are without self and attain patient endurance (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva would surpass the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva."
“Subhūti! It is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why does a bodhisattva not accept merit? “Subhūti!
"A Bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit he produces; therefore it is said that he does not 'receive' merit.
Suppose someone were to practice giving with the seven treasures of immeasurable worlds, yet their mind remained attached; the resulting merit would then be "with outflows" (sāsrava).
If the mind is free from attachment, it becomes "without outflows" (anāsrava); thus it is said that if someone knows all dharmas are without self, they attain the stage of patience (kṣānti).
"Non-self" refers to the absence of the two attachments to persons and phenomena.
"Patience" here is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is realized by Bodhisattvas at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Having attained this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, one differs from those who practice giving while abiding in signs; therefore, it is said that [this merit] surpasses the merit obtained by the aforementioned Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the statement "not receiving merit," it means not receiving tainted karmic rewards.
Subhūti then had another doubt:
"If one does not receive karmic rewards, how can one attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas?"
One should know that the retribution of outflows (*sāsrava*) should not be received, whereas the retribution free from outflows (*anāsrava*) is received without grasping (*anupādāna*).
"Grasping" refers to attachment; therefore, it is said that the merit performed by a Bodhisattva should not be clung to with craving.

24. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Receiving of Merit by the Emanation Body (Nirmāṇakāya). This doubt arises from the preceding section on not receiving merit: “Subhūti!... [as follows: 24. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Receiving of Merit by the Emanation Body. This doubt follows from the previous discussion on not receiving merit: “Subhūti!... [as follows:]
If someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down," that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata.
Those who come, go, sit, or lie down are the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) of the Tathāgata.
That which neither comes nor goes is the Dharmakāya.

Yet, when the Tathāgata formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, he did not accept karmic rewards; how then can there be the marks of going, coming, sitting, and reclining upon reaching the fruit, such that all sentient beings may make offerings and obtain merit?

Fearing that such doubts might arise, I have explained them to resolve them: it means that while the Tathāgata manifests movement through his functional application (*upāya*), the essence of the Dharma-body remains as it is, unmoving.

25. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Identity or Difference between the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya. Twenty-fifth: Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Identity or Difference between the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya. This doubt arises from the preceding [discussion]: "If dharmas have neither coming nor going, yet there is coming... [The Buddha said: "Subhūti!"
If a good son or a good daughter were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be numerous?"
Subhūti replied, “Very many, World-Honored One!

The preceding passage clarifies that while the coming and going of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) constitutes difference, the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is one because it is devoid of coming and going. Fearing that Subhūti might harbor views of oneness or difference, the Buddha therefore employs a parable to resolve this.
In the commentary, first, the identity and difference of the atoms of the world are raised to sever doubts; next, the self and dharmas of verbal expression are raised to transcend views.
Within the first section, there are three parts:
first, the identity and difference of the atoms of the world are indicated to reveal their lack of intrinsic nature.
To speak of the world is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya;
to speak of atoms is a metaphor for the Nirmāṇakāya.
The world is one, while the atoms are many.
When the realm is broken down into particles, the particles possess no distinct nature;
when the particles are joined to form the realm, the realm possesses no singular nature.

This is like the totality of phenomena arising as response: the response possesses no distinct nature, and the totality of the response is itself the phenomenon; the phenomenon possesses no singular nature.
Thus, the verse says:
"The transformation bodies of the Buddha come and go, while the Dharma-body is eternally unmoving; within this realm of reality (dharmadhātu), it is neither one nor different.
Yet, because the essence and function of the Tathāgata are mutually fused, he is able to be both one and different, and neither one nor different, possessing sovereign and unimpeded mastery.
"Why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as 'multitudes of atoms. Why is that?"
"The Buddha spoke of a multitude of subtle particles, yet they are not a multitude of subtle particles; they are merely named 'a multitude of subtle particles.
This explains that the subtle particles serve as a metaphor for the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which possesses no distinct intrinsic nature.

If one knows that the shattering of the world produces subtle particles (*paramāṇu*), yet these subtle particles are entirely the world itself, then the particles have no real nature; therefore it is said, "they are not subtle particles.
Because one speaks of "subtle particles" by departing from the attachment to their inherent nature, it is said, "this is called 'subtle particles'."
This metaphor illustrates that the arising of phenomena is itself the phenomenon; how could it be anything other than their very nature?
"World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata calls the trichiliocosm is not a world; it is merely named 'world'."

Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a single unified whole. Yet what the Tathāgata calls a single unified whole is not a single unified whole; it is merely designated as a "single unified whole."
"Subhūti! That which is a 'unified mass' (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is inexpressible; it is only that foolish commoners (bāla-pṛthagjana) greedily cling to such things.

This explains that the world, as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), lacks a single nature. If one knows that the world is formed by the aggregation of atoms (paramāṇu), then the world is entirely nothing but atoms; thus, the world has no real nature, and therefore it is said to "not be a world."
Because one speaks of the world by departing from the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, it is said: "This is called the world.
As for the "unified aggregate" (ekaghanākāra), it refers to the various particles combining to form a single world.
That which is not a "unified mark" is not a unified state resulting from attachment to intrinsic nature;
that which is called a "unified mark" is rather a unified state free from intrinsic nature.
This unified mark is inconceivable and inexpressible, yet ordinary beings fail to understand it and thus give rise to craving and attachment toward it.
This analogy should be entirely identical to the dharma; since the dharma is not separate from the analogy, how could there be any single nature? "Subhūti!
If someone were to say: "
"The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being,
and the view of a life-span. Subhūti, what do you think?
“Does this person understand the meaning of what I have taught?
“No, World-Honored One! This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.”

Why is this? The World-Honored One has said that the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."
The following section clarifies the abandonment of the two views of self and phenomena;
first, the abandonment of the view of self.
Now, as for the view of self, there is the view of a true self and the view of a deluded self.
The view of a false self is the deluded discrimination of the view of sentient beings;
the view of the true self is the vision of the Tathāgata, which is free from attachment.
Having abandoned all attachment, one manifests the views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span; this is seeing by means of non-seeing.
Deluded sentient beings believe that the Tathāgata truly possesses these four views; therefore, it is said that they do not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.

Since Subhūti understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught, he knows that all four views are non-existent and are merely false conceptualizations; thus, he says, "These are called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span."

“Subhūti! Those who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should know all dharmas in this way, see them in this way, and believe and understand them in this way, so that they do not give rise to the notion of dharmas.”
"Subhūti! That which is called the 'characteristic of dharmas'—the Tathāgata says it is not a characteristic of dharmas; it is merely named the 'characteristic of dharmas.
This next section is on departing from the view of dharmas.

Now, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, his primary aim is to cause sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta and to practice in accordance with the truth; therefore, upon hearing what the Tathāgata has taught, one should understand, perceive, believe, and resolve it in this way, without giving rise to the conceptualization of dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of non-arising dharmas," it means not grasping or attaching to dharmas.

Dharmas are fundamentally free from characteristics; the Tathāgata speaks in accordance with their true nature, and thus says that what is called the "characteristic of dharmas" is in fact not a characteristic of dharmas—it is only designated as such.
Although this passage serves as a commentary on being free from attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), it also summarizes the practice of descending into and abiding in the correct conduct.
This is because at the beginning of the sutra, Subhūti asked:
"If a person has resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, how should they abide?"
"How should one subdue the mind?
The Tathāgata replied:
"One should abide thus, and thus subdue the mind."
Therefore, the conclusion now states:
"One who has resolved upon Bodhicitta thus knows, sees, and believes in all dharmas. This concludes the section on "abiding thus";
"not giving rise to the marks of dharmas" concludes the section on "subduing the deluded mind."

26. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Lack of Merit in the Dharma-Preaching of an Emanation Body (Nirmāṇakāya). This doubt arises from the preceding analogy of the dust, concerning the emanation body as something distinct [from the Buddha] that comes forth: "Subhūti!..."

If someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and takes up even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra—upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others—their merit would surpass that of the former.
"How does one expound the Dharma for others?
Without grasping at appearances, remaining as suchness, unmoving.
This passage consists of three sections; the first, regarding the giving of the seven treasures throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, is a provisional analogy used for comparison.
From the passage beginning with "If there is a good man... onwards, it clarifies that the merit of upholding and expounding [the sutra] is superior.

From the passage beginning with "How does one expound it for others? onwards, this explains why the merit is superior. Thus, while the sutra text only clarifies the merit of upholding and expounding, the treatise states that the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) who preaches the Dharma possesses immeasurable merit. This is because the transformation Buddha is the teacher who expounds the sutra, while those who uphold and expound are the ones who propagate the sutra; the sutra being propagated was spoken by the Buddha, and what the Buddha spoke is free from the characteristics of verbal expression; therefore, its merit is immeasurable.
If those who propagate the sutra can remain free from attachment, their merit will surpass that [of the former].
"Suchness" (tathatā) is the principle of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Since the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is identical to the Dharma-body, it neither departs nor arrives; therefore, it is immovable.
27. Severing Entry into Quiescence: Doubts Regarding How the Dharma is Taught. This doubt arises from the preceding discussion on "teaching" and "immovability": "For what reason?"

Since it was stated above that suchness is immovable, and thus the Buddha eternally dwells in the world preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, for what reason is it said that the Tathāgata enters nirvana?
Fearing that such doubts might arise, he spoke a verse to resolve them, saying:
"All conditioned phenomena Are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
Like dew and likewise like lightning— One should contemplate them in this way."
"All conditioned phenomena" refers to all worldly phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
The Buddha, having been born among humans, manifested the appearance of arising and ceasing; he, too, belonged to the category of conditioned and impermanent phenomena.
The dharma of impermanence is false and unreal; therefore, it is illustrated by six metaphors: a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and lightning.

Those who should practice such contemplation do so through *prajñā*, the wondrous wisdom; with this wondrous wisdom, they contemplate conditioned phenomena as being like dreams, illusions, and the rest.
Since that which is capable of contemplation is wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), that which is contemplated is nothing other than the wondrous object.
The "wondrous object" refers to the three truths within a single object;
the "wondrous wisdom" refers to the three contemplations within a single mind.
The three contemplations are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*).
The three truths are the ultimate (*paramārtha*), the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and the middle.
That is to say, contemplating conditioned phenomena as being devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics is called emptiness.
That which lacks nothing is called the "provisional" (prajñapti);
that which is neither empty nor provisional is called the "middle" (madhyama).
As for "truth" (satya), it refers to that which is examined and found to be real and not false.

One gives rise to contemplation based on the ultimate truth and uses that contemplation to illumine the conventional truth. Since the truths are both one and three, how could the contemplation be sequential in its illumination?
Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate thus."
To be able to contemplate in this way is to realize that the *nirmāṇakāya* is itself the *dharmakāya*, and that impermanence is itself permanence.
Although it is the *dharmakāya*, it does not obstruct *nirvāṇa*; thus, permanence is itself impermanence.

It is precisely because the Tathāgata has ultimately realized the dharma that is neither eternal nor impermanent that he is thus able to be both eternal and impermanent. This means that while he is in *nirvāṇa* all day long, he is also preaching the Dharma all day long; he abides neither in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and is beyond the reach of thought or speculation.

Throughout the beginning and end of this sutra, the phrase "Thus" (evam) is employed; it begins with "Thus dwelling" and "Thus subduing the mind," and at every subsequent stage it says "Thus," until here it again states "Thus contemplating. The *Śāstra* then explains:
"Because it is the correct contemplation of wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), one knows that wondrous wisdom is truly the central theme of this entire sutra."
The Main Body concludes.

Regarding the Dissemination Section: After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month in the tenth year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor issued an edict ordering that all monastics throughout the realm study and master the three sūtras—the Heart Sūtra, the Diamond Sūtra, and the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra—lecturing upon them by day and practicing meditative concentration by night.
He further issued an edict:

"Gather the monastic assemblies of the Chan and Teaching schools from all prefectures at Tianjie Shanshi Chan Monastery to collate and edit the ancient commentaries on the Three Sutras. Once their interpretations are finalized, circulate them throughout the empire to promote their widespread preservation and transmission."

We humbly reflect that Your Majesty, as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), governs by virtue of your long-accumulated vows; having personally received the entrustment of the Holy Mountain, you cause the teachings to circulate and sustain the life of wisdom—how exceedingly fortunate we are!

Thereupon, we, the ministers-monks Zongle and others, though our talents be dull and mediocre, dare to exhaust our sincere hearts to record what we have heard throughout our lives and venture to provide these annotations.

Once the commentary was completed, on the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the eleventh year, we presented it at the palace gate. After His Majesty had perused it in the Huagai Hall, he approved the work and issued an imperial decree to carve woodblocks for its circulation throughout the world.

Nevertheless, these three sutras are all essential for the ultimate investigation of the mind; their efficacy lies in shattering delusive emotions to reveal the true nature. Furthermore, the merit of their circulation is no small matter: above, they provide secret support for the royal order, and below, they benefit all living beings. This is not merely a blessing for our own school at this one time, but is truly the supreme blessing for all under heaven throughout ten thousand generations.
Respectfully recorded by the monk Zongle on the [blank] day of the first month in the eleventh year of Hongwu.
